name: Grounding and Hallucination Checks
question: Does the retrieved text actually support what the answer says?
summary: A grounding check verifies, after generation, that each claim in an answer is supported by the context it was given. The answer is split into atomic claims, a checker scores each claim against the retrieved passages, and answers with unsupported claims are regenerated, flagged or refused. Checkers range from a full LLM judge to small fine-tuned models such as MiniCheck or HHEM that are fast enough for every answer; a cascade sends only the unsure claims to the LLM. The threshold trades errors that reach users against good answers refused. Making the model cite its sources is covered by Citations and Grounded Answers (module 18), and other output checks by Post-LLM Guardrails; this technique is the detector and how to tune it.
useCases: RAG answers about fees, limits, eligibility or policy terms
Summaries of contracts, claims files or medical notes
Any high-volume assistant where a wrong fact has a cost

items.detail: one checkable fact per claim; long answers hide errors in the middle
LLM judge, NLI model, or a small fact-checker (MiniCheck, HHEM)
support score below which a claim is flagged; tune on labelled examples
share of good answers flagged; each may become a refusal
regenerate with the bad claims named, flag for review, or refuse safely

steps: Label 300–500 answers as supported or not to get a test set
Split answers into claims and score each with a small checker
Tune the threshold, and escalate the unsure band to an LLM judge
Regenerate once, then refuse; track errors reaching users and good answers refused
pitfalls: Checking against the model’s own knowledge instead of the retrieved text
A threshold picked without labelled data, so good answers are refused all day
Judging the whole long answer at once, so one wrong figure slips through
remember: Split into claims, check each against the context, tune the threshold on labels.
caption: Illustrative: Suraksha Health, a fictional insurer, checks 10,000 policy answers a day.

steps.title: Split the answer into claims
steps.text: Suraksha Health, a fictional insurer, answers 10,000 policy questions a day. A draft such as “Cataract is covered after a 2-year waiting period, up to ₹40,000 per eye” holds two claims, and each is checked on its own.

steps.title: Score each claim with a small checker
steps.text: A fact-checking model scores whether the retrieved policy text supports each claim. It is fast, about 150 ms, and costs about ₹0.03 an answer.

steps.title: Set the threshold
steps.text: At 0.5 the checker catches 88% of unsupported answers but flags 6% of good ones. Lower thresholds catch more and flag more.

steps.title: Escalate the unsure band
steps.text: Claims scored between 0.2 and 0.8, about 20% of answers, go to an LLM judge. The cascade catches 93% and wrongly flags only 3%.

steps.title: Regenerate, then refuse
steps.text: A flagged draft is regenerated with the unsupported claims named; if it still fails, the user gets a safe “could not confirm” reply.

steps.title: Watch the rates
steps.text: Of about 600 answers a day with an unsupported claim, about 42 still get through; about 85 good answers are refused. Both go on a weekly dashboard.

pros: Catches unsupported facts before users see them
Claim-level scores show exactly what is wrong
Small checkers are fast and cheap enough for every answer
Cascade keeps LLM-judge cost to the unsure cases
cons: Only checks against the retrieved text, not the truth
Claim splitting can drop or merge facts
avoidWhen: Open-ended creative output with no source to check against
As a substitute for fixing retrieval that misses the right passage

practice.scenario: Suraksha Health, a fictional insurer, answers 10,000 policy questions a day with RAG, and about 600 answers contain a claim the policy text does not support, such as a wrong sub-limit. It splits each draft into claims, scores them with a small fact-checking model in about 150 ms, sends the unsure 20% to an LLM judge, regenerates flagged drafts once and otherwise replies “could not confirm”. Unsupported answers reaching customers fall from 600 to about 42 a day, with about 85 good answers refused.

industries.use: Waiting periods, sub-limits and exclusions stated in answers
Fees, interest rates and eligibility quoted to customers
Summaries of discharge notes checked against the source record

practice.analogy: A proofreader who ticks each sentence of a report only if they can put a finger on the line in the source file that says it.

library.name: Vectara HHEM
library.what: An open hallucination evaluation model that scores whether a hypothesis is supported by a premise.

practice.note: The HHEM model loads with trust_remote_code; check its model card for the current usage and licence. Tune the 0.5 threshold on your own labelled answers.

samples.code:
from transformers import AutoModelForSequenceClassification

model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
    "vectara/hallucination_evaluation_model", trust_remote_code=True)

policy = ("Cataract surgery is covered after a waiting period of 24 months. "
          "The limit is Rs 25,000 per eye.")
claims = ["Cataract is covered after a two-year waiting period.",
          "The limit is Rs 40,000 per eye."]

scores = model.predict([(policy, c) for c in claims])     # 0 = unsupported, 1 = supported
for c, s in zip(claims, scores.tolist()):
    print(f"{s:.2f}", "OK  " if s >= 0.5 else "FLAG", c)

numericDrill.question: 600 of 10,000 daily answers are unsupported. A checker catches 88% of them and flags 6% of the 9,400 good answers. How many answers are flagged in total each day?
numericDrill.answer: Caught: 0.88 × 600 = 528. False flags: 0.06 × 9,400 = 564. Total flagged 528 + 564 = 1,092, and 72 unsupported answers get through.

interview.question: How would you detect hallucinations in a RAG answer?
interview.answer: Split the answer into atomic claims, score each against the retrieved passages with an NLI or fact-checking model, escalate unsure scores to an LLM judge, and regenerate or refuse answers with unsupported claims. Tune the threshold on labelled examples.

interview.question: Why check claim by claim?
interview.answer: A long answer can be mostly right with one wrong figure; whole-answer judging often misses it. Claim-level scores also show exactly what to fix.

mistakes.fix: Tune it on a few hundred labelled answers
Regenerate once with the bad claims named, then refuse
